As of 310 AM EDT Thursday...

KEY MESSAGE 1...Above-normal temperatures with dry conditions 
prevail through Friday.

Latest WX analysis indicates broad upper-level ridging across 
the southeast CONUS, extending offshore into the western 
Atlantic. An upstream deep closed low is situated over the 
central and southern High Plains early this morning. At the 
surface, ~1022 mb high pressure is centered just off the Mid-
Atlantic coast, ridging inland just to our south across east-
central NC.

The surface ridge will shift farther offshore today, becoming 
centered along the coastal Carolinas through Friday. Meanwhile, 
the upper ridge will build over the Eastern Seaboard today into 
tonight; the resulting height rises and S-SW flow aloft will 
push temperatures well above normal over the next couple of 
days. Forecast highs today remain in the mid-to-upper 80s to 
near 90F inland, with low-to-mid 80s along the coast. After a 
mild night with lows in the 60s, Friday will be even warmer, 
reaching the upper 80s to lower 90s. These values are roughly 
10-15°F above average for early October and certainly qualify as
"unseasonably warm." Record highs for Oct 1-2 are in the mid- 
to-upper 90s, so record highs are generally not expected to be 
broken, though Norfolk (ORF) could get close. Record highs for 
Friday are again included below for reference.

KEY MESSAGE 2...An unsettled weather pattern with cooler and 
wetter conditions is likely this weekend, followed by a gradual 
drying trend and cool temperatures next week.

An increasingly unsettled pattern still looks to take shape for
the weekend into early next week. The previously referenced 
upper closed low will lift E-NE across the mid-Mississippi and 
Tennessee River Valleys through Friday. The system is expected 
to open up tonight into Friday as it ingests the mid-level 
remnants of TC Polo before being absorbed into a northern- 
stream trough. That trough then digs across the interior 
Northeast into the northern Mid- Atlantic Friday night into the
weekend. This dampens the Southeast ridge and allows an influx 
of Gulf and Pacific moisture across the Gulf Coast and Mid- 
South, reaching our region over the weekend.

The attendant cold front drops through the area Saturday 
afternoon and evening, likely stalling across southern sections 
into Sunday morning. An axis of increasing moisture will
accompany the front, with strong model consensus showing 
precipitable water values climbing to 1.5-2.0" by Saturday 
night/Sunday. Mostly cloudy skies and scattered to numerous 
showers will accompany the initial frontal passage and wind 
shift on Saturday. Instability remains meager and lapse rates 
remain shallow, minimizing any threat for strong storms, though
gusty N-NE winds are likely post-frontal. The bulk of the QPF 
and more widespread overrunning rainfall arrive Saturday night 
through Monday morning, clearing from NW to SE. 00Z/01 ensemble 
probabilities for 1"+ of total rainfall are displaced farther 
north along/east of the developing CAD wedge axis per the EPS 
and CMC, while the GEFS remains suppressed farther south. A 
second, more potent shortwave dropping out of the Canadian 
Prairies and Upper Midwest will push a reinforcing cold front 
across the region Sunday night into Monday, bringing lingering 
precipitation to an end.

In terms of temperatures, the unseasonably warm readings of the
next 48 hours will be a distant memory by the weekend. Cloud 
cover, precipitation, and persistent onshore flow will cap high
temperatures in the mid-to-upper 60s for most areas Saturday 
and Sunday (mid to upper 70s across the far south). Guidance 
remains in good agreement on a sharp cool down accompanied by a
strong push of drier air, as chilly high pressure builds in 
from the north through the middle of next week. This keeps 
temperatures below normal for much of next week, with highs in 
the 60s and lows in the 40s and 50s Tuesday and Wednesday. LREF 
probabilities even hint at a chance for lows dipping into the 
upper 30s across our NW Piedmont zones by Wednesday morning.
